cards.front: What four kinds of member may an interface declare?
cards.back: Constants, abstract methods, static methods and default methods (private helpers since Java 9)
cards.extra: No instance fields and no constructors — an interface has no state to initialise.
cards.example:
interface Ex {
  int LIMIT = 10;                                   // constant
  void run();                                       // abstract
  static int twice(int n) { return 2 * n; }         // static
  default String label() { return "p" + secret(); } // default
  private String secret() { return "!"; } }         // private since Java 9

cards.front: What modifiers does an interface variable implicitly have?
cards.back: public static final — and its visibility cannot be changed
cards.extra: String LED = "LED"; in an interface is a constant. Writing private or omitting final does not alter that.
cards.example:
interface Ex {
  int LIMIT = 3; // implicitly public static final
  // private int HIDDEN = 1; // error: visibility cannot be changed
}

cards.front: What modifiers can an interface method never have?
cards.extra: protected has no meaning without inheritance of state, and final contradicts the point of an abstract method.
cards.example:
interface Ex {
  void run(); // implicitly public abstract
  // protected void p(); // error
  // final void f() {} // error
}

cards.extra: An interface exists to be implemented; final would forbid the only thing it is for.
cards.example:
interface Open { }
// final interface Closed { }  // error: illegal combination of modifiers: interface and final

cards.front: How does a class take on an interface, and how does an interface take on another?
cards.back: A class implements; an interface extends another interface
cards.extra: An interface can extend several interfaces at once; a class can implement any number of them.
cards.example:
interface Base { void f(); }
interface Child extends Base { void g(); }
class Ex implements Child { public void f() {} public void g() {} }

cards.front: If Box extends HasColor, what must a class implementing Box provide?
cards.back: The methods of both — the inherited getColor() and its own getHeight()
cards.extra: Inheritance in interfaces is additive: the child interface's contract includes the parent's.
cards.example:
interface HasColor { String getColor(); }
interface Box extends HasColor { int getHeight(); }
class Carton implements Box { public String getColor() { return "brown"; } public int getHeight() { return 3; } }
class Ex { static void demo() { Box b = new Carton(); System.out.println(b.getColor() + b.getHeight()); } }

cards.front: What happens when an abstract class implements an interface?
cards.back: It inherits the abstract and default methods but may leave the abstract ones unimplemented
cards.extra: That is the standard way to provide a partial implementation — the abstract class absorbs the boilerplate, concrete subclasses finish it.
cards.example:
interface Api { void required(); default String label() { return "api"; } }
abstract class Base implements Api { } // required() left to a concrete subclass
class Impl extends Base { public void required() {} }
class Ex { static void demo() { System.out.println(new Impl().label()); } }

cards.front: Why were default methods added in Java 8?
cards.back: Backward compatibility: adding an abstract method to a published interface would break every existing implementation
cards.extra: A default method supplies a body, so old classes keep compiling; the library can evolve without a major version break.
cards.example:
interface Api { void existing(); default int size() { return 0; } }
class Impl implements Api { public void existing() {} } // old implementer unchanged
class Ex { static void demo() { Api a = new Impl(); System.out.println(a.size()); } }

cards.front: How do interfaces give Java multiple inheritance?
cards.back: A class can implement many interfaces, so it takes on many types — but still only one superclass
cards.extra: It inherits contracts, not state, which is why the diamond problem does not apply the same way.
cards.example:
interface A { void a(); }
interface B { void b(); }
class Base { }
class Ex extends Base implements A, B { public void a() {} public void b() {}
  static void demo() { Ex x = new Ex(); A a = x; B b = x; Base base = x; } }

cards.front: How does an interface produce polymorphism?
cards.back: One interface type, many implementations — the overridden method that runs is chosen by the object's runtime type
cards.extra: A List<Shape> holding Circle and Square prints differently per element without a type test.
cards.example:
interface Shape { String name(); }
class Circle implements Shape { public String name() { return "circle"; } }
class Square implements Shape { public String name() { return "square"; } }
class Ex { static void demo() { Shape s = new Circle(); System.out.println(s.name());
  s = new Square(); System.out.println(s.name()); } }
